--- title: "Github" engine: knitr --- GitHub is an online open-source platform for building, storing and collaborating on software projects. It is based on Git, an open-source version control system that keeps track of changes to files and code. GitHub allows you to store your Git projects, called repositories, in the cloud. It also provides tools for collaboration, version control and sharing your work with others. GitHub Desktop provides a graphical interface for working with Git, making it easier to manage your repositories without using the command line. You will use Github throughout this module to store and submit your R code and projects. ## Create a Github Account 1. Go to Github 2. Select Sign up and create an account 3. Choose a suitable username - this will be visible to others 4. Verify your email address when prompted 5. Sign into Github ## Install Github Desktop Download and install GitHub Desktop from [desktop.github.com.](https://github.com/apps/desktop) Once installed: 1. Open GitHub Desktop. 2.Select Sign in to GitHub.com. 3.Sign in using your GitHub account. 4. Allow GitHub Desktop to access your account when prompted. ## Create Your First Repository A repository (repo) is a folder containing your project files and their version history. You can create a repository directly from GitHub Desktop: 1. Select Create a New Repository. 2. Give it a name, such as MS6071-R-Labs. 3. Choose a local folder where you want to store the project. 4. Select Create Repository. You can then select Publish repository to upload the repository to GitHub. When publishing, make sure the repository is Private unless you have been instructed otherwise. ## Working with Your Repository Your GitHub repository will exist in two places: - Local repository — a folder on your computer. - Remote repository — the copy stored on GitHub. When you work on your R files, you will normally work in the local repository. ## Commit Your Changes After creating or changing files, open GitHub Desktop. The Changes tab will show the files that have been added or modified. 1. Review the changes. 2. Enter a short description in the Summary box, for example: 3. Complete Lab 1 4. Select Commit to main. A commit is a saved snapshot of your project. It provides a record of what changed and when. It is good practice to make regular, meaningful commits rather than waiting until the end of a project. ## Push Your Changes to GitHub Committing saves the changes to your local repository. To upload them to GitHub, you must push the changes. After committing: 1. Select Push origin in GitHub Desktop. 2. Your changes will be uploaded to the GitHub repository. 3. You can then log in to GitHub in your browser and see the updated files. A useful way to remember the process is: Edit → Commit → Push ## Pull Changes from GitHub If the repository has been changed on GitHub or by another collaborator, you can download the latest changes to your computer. In GitHub Desktop, select: Fetch origin → Pull origin This updates your local repository with the latest version from GitHub. ## Additional resources * Github Instructions [website](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/start-your-journey).
